title: The strong law of large numbers
statement: \begin{gathered} X_1, X_2, \dots \ \text{i.i.d.}, \quad \mathbb{E}|X_1| < \infty \\ \Longrightarrow \ \bar X_n = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} X_i \to \mathbb{E} X_1 \ \text{almost surely} \end{gathered}
assumptions: The X_i have the same law.
The X_i are pairwise independent (Etemadi). Full independence is the classical condition.
proof: Truncate: Y_k = X_k 1{|X_k| ≤ k}. Integrability gives Σ P(X_k ≠ Y_k) < ∞, so X_k = Y_k for all large k (Borel–Cantelli). Chebyshev's inequality on a geometric subsequence n_j = ⌊α^j⌋ with α > 1 gives almost sure convergence of the truncated means. For X ≥ 0, monotonicity covers the indices between the n_j. Then split X = X⁺ − X⁻.
reference: R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Cambridge University Press, 2019, Theorem 2.4.1. N. Etemadi, An elementary proof of the strong law of large numbers, Z. Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie verw. Gebiete 55 (1981) 119–122.
counterexample: The zeta law with s = 1.8 has E[X] = ∞. Then X̄_n → ∞ almost surely, so no finite limit exists.

title: The central limit theorem and the CLT interval
assumptions: The variance σ² is finite and positive.
The coverage 0.95 of the interval X̄_n ± 1.96 s_n/√n is a limit as n → ∞. A bound for a given n needs more, for example E|X|³ < ∞ (Berry–Esseen).
proof: Let φ be the characteristic function of X_1 − μ. Then φ(u) = 1 − σ²u²/2 + o(u²), and the characteristic function of the normalised sum is φ(t/(σ√n))^n. Its limit is e^(−t²/2). Lévy's continuity theorem gives convergence in law. Slutsky's lemma replaces σ by s_n.
reference: R. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., 2019, Theorem 3.4.1. B. V. Gnedenko and A. N. Kolmogorov, Limit Distributions for Sums of Independent Random Variables, Addison-Wesley, 1954.
counterexample: The zeta law with s = 2.5 has a finite mean and an infinite variance. Then (S_n − nμ)/n^(2/3) converges in law to a stable law with index 1.5, not to a normal law. Thus the CLT interval has no coverage guarantee. The block coverage in the diagnostics shows the effect in a run.

title: Consistency of the estimator and exactness of rejection
assumptions: Each replicate draws exactly from the model law.
For rejection: p and q each sum to 1, and p(k) ≤ M q(k) for every k. The acceptance uniform is independent of the proposal.
proof: Unbiasedness follows from the linearity of expectation, and consistency from the strong law. For rejection, P(accept, Y = k) = q(k) p(k)/(M q(k)) = p(k)/M. The sum over k gives P(accept) = 1/M. Divide to get P(Y = k | accept) = p(k).
reference: L. Devroye, Non-Uniform Random Variate Generation, Springer, 1986, chapter II. S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation: Algorithms and Analysis, Springer, 2007, chapter II.
counterexample: If M is too small, the accepted values follow min(p, Mq) after normalisation, not p. The estimator is then consistent for the wrong quantity.

title: Monte Carlo error and the zero-hit bound
assumptions: σ_g² = Var g(X) is finite for Var θ̂_n = σ_g²/n.
For the zero-hit bound, each replicate shows the event independently with the same probability p.
proof: The variance of a sum of independent terms is the sum of their variances, so Var θ̂_n = σ_g²/n for any dimension of X. For the bound: P(0 hits) = (1 − p)^n, which is at most α if and only if p ≥ 1 − α^(1/n). Thus a test at level α rejects every p above the bound.
reference: S. Asmussen and P. W. Glynn, Stochastic Simulation, 2007, chapter III. J. A. Hanley and A. Lippman-Hand, If nothing goes wrong, is everything all right? JAMA 249 (1983) 1743–1745.
counterexample: If replicates reuse 16 streams, the draws repeat and are not independent. The formula s/√n then understates the error by a factor near √(n/16), and the intervals cover the reference less often.
